description_full: AMC Global Media Inc., an entertainment company, distributes contents in the United States, Europe, and internationally. It operates in two segments, Domestic Operations and International. The Domestic Operations segment operates programming networks, such as AMC, We TV, BBCA, IFC, and SundanceTV; provides streaming services, including AMC+ and Acorn TV, Shudder, Sundance Now, ALLBLK, HIDIVE, and All Reality targeted subscription streaming services; produces original programming for its programming services and third parties; and licenses programming. This segment is also involved in the film distribution business comprising Independent Film Company, RLJE Films, and Shudder; and technical services business for programming networks. The International segment operates a portfolio of channels. The company was formerly known as AMC Networks Inc. and changed its name to AMC Global Media Inc. in April 2026. AMC Global Media Inc. was founded in 1980 and is headquartered in New York, New York.

financial_summary: AMC Global Media Inc. is a small-cap communication services business with a $346M market cap on $2.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -9% over the past three years and -1% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 4% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $272M in free cash flow — roughly 12 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.42× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 5.5× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 0.8× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 5.2% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 6.5% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.3× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 6% operating margin is roughly in line with the Communication Services median (9%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.28x its revenue share).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-31.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.06 across 169 companies in the universe; the top four hold 36% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 51% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 29% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 35% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 50% and a beta of 1.14, it moves roughly with the market.
About $6.3M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 51% in the 2020 crash and 68% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 89% below its DCF fair value of $76.42, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 63%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $50.81 to $117 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Communication Services peers: P/E 3.2 vs 14.9, EV/EBITDA 6.4 vs 9.4 and P/FCF 1.3 vs 11.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 16% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 78.7% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 8.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 6 covering analysts target $9.67 on average, 15% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 4% falls short of the cost of capital of 7.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.76).
It converts 12% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 3.42x.
ROE of 9% is amplified by 4.0x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 1.1% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 5.5x net debt to EBITDA ($502.4M of cash against $1.8B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 0.8x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.70 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
The value-trap profile is elevated (66/100); see the breakdown below.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -9.3% over 3 years, -3.9% over 5 years and -1.1% over 10 years, so the decline is deepening, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 13%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -17.3% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.4x depreciation (1.4% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders own 6.5%, meaningful skin in the game, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 5.2% a year to shareholders (5.2% in buybacks).
The share count has shrunk 2.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
Short interest is elevated at 18.1% of the float, 8.4 days to cover.
people: With about 1,675 employees, each generates about $1.4M of revenue, 2.3x the Communication Services median, and productivity has risen 4.9% a year.
That works out to $163K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $8.3M (6x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (10/10, lower is better).
